name: Innocence Project (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: wrongly convicted people in US prisons and their families (exonerations, reforms that prevent wrongful convictions, compensation).
summary: The Innocence Project is a US legal organisation (31.5 million dollars spent in the year to June 2025) that frees wrongly convicted people, mostly with DNA evidence, campaigns for laws that prevent wrongful convictions and compensate exonerees, and supports the Innocence Network's groups. Its spending over fiscal years 2021-2025 is counted as a past average over what those years achieved: about a third of the credit for its 24 exonerations (the years in prison they would still have served, the deaths prison causes, and compensation counted as a transfer, the exoneree's gain less the taxpayers' cost), shared with pro bono law firms that give about as much as it spends, about a third of a small cut in wrongful imprisonment from the eyewitness, interrogation, discovery and compensation laws it won or defended, and a small share of other innocence groups' exonerations; every branch is discounted for missing data. The result is about 0.0005 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars: its casework costs about two million dollars per exoneration, each freeing one person from about a dozen more years in prison; the reforms of the window remove only about 1% of the country's wrongful imprisonment; and the next dollar counts at a third of the average as it holds over three years of spending in reserve. The model's own ranges span more than a thousandfold, so the result is mostly uncertainty; the biggest are how many people in US prisons are innocent, how much the window's reforms cut that, and the Innocence Project's share of the coalitions behind the reforms.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Innocence Project

resources.title: ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, The Innocence Project Inc (EIN 32-0077563), Forms 990 by fiscal year
Gross et al. (2014), Rate of false conviction of criminal defendants who are sentenced to death, PNAS

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: The Innocence Project's spending, averaged over fiscal years 2021-2025 (the years whose exonerations and reforms are counted) in 2025 prices, with its share of management and fundraising. From its Forms 990 (IRS e-file).

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: Clients freed from prison in the window, the wrongful imprisonment the window's reforms act on, and other innocence groups' exonerations, as reported by the Innocence Project, the Bureau of Justice Statistics and the National Registry of Exonerations.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What freeing a person, or sparing one a wrongful conviction, is worth: life satisfaction and the deaths a year in prison causes (the site's shared incarceration figures), executions averted, and compensation as a transfer.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Per branch: trust in the evidence, what others would have done, the Innocence Project's share of the resources, delivery, and the site's discount for missing data; plus the side effects as shares of each branch.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Clients exonerated, fiscal years 2021-2025
rows.explainer: 24 exonerations in five years, 2 to 7 a year. Its count of people 'helped free' rose from more than 237 (2021 return) to more than 253 (2025 return), about the same pace.

rows.label: Share of the exonerated who were still in prison until the Innocence Project's work freed them
rows.explainer: Some clients are exonerated after release on parole, when the years in prison are already over: one of fiscal year 2024's was cleared 47 years after his conviction, having served 7.5 (annual report 2024, pp. 4-6). Others were released by the Innocence Project's own work inside the window and exonerated later (Rosa Jimenez, released in 2021, exonerated in 2023), which counts as freed. Most clients are serving long sentences for murder or rape (16 years served on average, data page). Our judgment: 80%, from 60% to 95%.

source.title: Innocence Project, Annual Report 2024, client stories (pp. 4-6 of the PDF)

rows.label: People freed from wrongful imprisonment a year (average of fiscal years 2021-2025)
rows.explainer: Clients freed from prison by the Innocence Project's lawyers in an average year of the window: the exonerations times the share still in prison, over five years.

rows.label: People in US state and federal prisons, yearend 2023

source.title: Bureau of Justice Statistics, Prisoners in 2023 (highlights)
source.quote: The U.S. prison population was 1,254,200 at yearend 2023, an increase of 24,100 persons (up 2%) from 2022 (1,230,100).

rows.explainer: The prison population the reforms act on: people serving sentences in state and federal prisons (jails, mostly unconvicted people, are left out).

rows.label: Share of people in US prisons who are innocent of the crime they are held for
rows.explainer: No one knows the rate for prisons as a whole. The one careful estimate is for death sentences: at least 4.1% would be exonerated if all stayed under sentence indefinitely (Gross et al. 2014), and the authors warn it can't be carried over to other convictions. DNA retesting of old Virginia murder and sexual-assault convictions excluded the convicted person in about 5% (Roman et al. 2012, Urban Institute), and about 6% of Pennsylvania prisoners surveyed said they were innocent (Loeffler, Hyatt and Ridgeway 2019), against much lower rates for the pleas behind most prison terms. Our judgment: 2%, from 0.5% to 5%.

source.title: Gross, O'Brien, Hu and Kennedy (2014), Rate of false conviction of criminal defendants who are sentenced to death, PNAS 111(20): 7230-7235

rows.label: Years of wrongful imprisonment served in the US each year
rows.explainer: The innocent people in prison at any time, which is also the years of wrongful imprisonment served each year.

rows.label: Eyewitness and facial-recognition laws won: share of the US population covered
rows.explainer: Indiana's 2025 eyewitness identification law with its facial-recognition limits (2% of the US) and Maryland's 2024 law on police use of facial recognition (1.8%), with smaller wins elsewhere (annual reports 2024 and 2025). Our judgment: 4%, from 2% to 7%.

source.title: Innocence Project, Annual Report 2025, policy wins (pp. 13-15 of the PDF)

rows.label: Share of wrongful convictions with a mistaken witness identification
rows.explainer: 26% of 2024's exonerations involved a mistaken witness identification (National Registry of Exonerations via Criminal Legal News); 62% of the Innocence Project's DNA cases did (data page). Most wrongful convictions are never exonerated, so the share is a range: 26%, from 20% to 40%.

source.title: Criminal Legal News (April 2025), Nearly 150 Exonerations in 2024 (the National Registry of Exonerations' 2024 report)

rows.label: Cut in mistaken identifications from the procedures the laws require (laboratory evidence)
rows.explainer: Blind administration, fair fillers and recording the witness's confidence are recommended on laboratory evidence that they cut mistaken identifications, with some loss of correct ones (Wells et al. 2020, Law and Human Behavior). Our judgment: 25% as the studies show it, from 10% to 40%; whether it holds in the field is pol_evidence_adj.

source.title: Wells et al. (2020), Policy and procedure recommendations for the collection and preservation of eyewitness identification evidence, Law and Human Behavior 44(1): 3-36

rows.label: Interrogation laws won (bans on deceiving children, recording): share of the US population covered
rows.explainer: Ten states have banned police deception in interrogating children since Illinois in 2021 (NPR, October 2024). Which states they are, and their population share, is our reading: 25% of the US population, from 15% to 40%.

source.title: NPR (21 October 2024), police deception bans: ten states have passed laws banning police from lying to children in interrogations since Illinois in 2021

rows.label: Share of wrongful convictions with a false confession by a child
rows.explainer: False confessions are in 15% of 2024's exonerations (National Registry via Criminal Legal News), and children give a large minority of them; the bans cover only children. Our judgment: 3% of wrongful convictions, from 1% to 6%.

source.title: Criminal Legal News (April 2025), Nearly 150 Exonerations in 2024 (the National Registry of Exonerations' 2024 report)

rows.label: Cut in children's false confessions from the bans
rows.explainer: Deception (false evidence ploys) is the tactic most tied to false confessions in laboratory and case studies. Our judgment: the bans remove 30%, from 10% to 50%.

source.title: Kassin et al. (2010), Police-induced confessions: risk factors and recommendations, Law and Human Behavior 34(1): 3-38

rows.label: Population of New York, 1 July 2024

source.title: US Census Bureau, Vintage 2024 population estimates (press release, December 2024), Table 1

rows.explainer: The state's population, for its share of the country.

rows.label: Population of Texas, 1 July 2024

source.title: US Census Bureau, Vintage 2024 population estimates (press release, December 2024), Table 1
source.quote: for a total population of 31,290,831 in 2024

rows.explainer: The state's population, for its share of the country.

rows.label: Discovery laws defended against rollback (New York, Texas): share of the US population
rows.explainer: New York's and Texas's share of the US population, where the 2025 attempts to weaken discovery failed or were cut back (annual report 2025, p. 15).

rows.label: Share of wrongful convictions with evidence the defence didn't see
rows.explainer: Official misconduct taints 71% of 2024's exonerations (National Registry via Criminal Legal News); concealing exculpatory evidence is one kind of it. Our judgment: 35% involve evidence that full discovery would have shown, from 20% to 50%.

source.title: Criminal Legal News (April 2025), Nearly 150 Exonerations in 2024 (the National Registry of Exonerations' 2024 report)

rows.label: Cut in those wrongful convictions that open-file discovery brings, times the share a rollback would have undone
rows.explainer: Full and early discovery lets the defence find what was withheld; a rollback would have undone part of it, and only part might have passed without the defence (New York's protections remain 'largely intact'). Our judgment: 30% cut × 20% undone = 6%, from 2% to 15%.

source.title: Innocence Project, Annual Report 2025, policy wins (pp. 13-15 of the PDF)

rows.label: Other laws and precedents of the window: share of wrongful imprisonment removed
rows.explainer: The rest of the window's wins: in fiscal year 2024 alone 15 laws in 41 states with partners (annual report 2024), on DNA access, forensic science commissions, informants and new evidence of innocence (Tennessee 2025), and court precedents from strategic litigation (Glossip v. Oklahoma on false testimony, juvenile confessions, discovery of bias evidence; more than 35 amicus briefs in 2025). Most widen paths to relief or bar one kind of evidence in one state. Our judgment: 0.2%, from 0.05% to 0.6%.

source.title: Innocence Project, Annual Report 2024, policy wins

rows.label: Share of the country's wrongful imprisonment the reforms won or defended in fiscal years 2021-2025 remove
rows.formula: pol_ew_pop_share * pol_ew_cause_share * pol_ew_cut + pol_int_pop_share * pol_int_cause_share * pol_int_cut + pol_disc_pop_share * pol_disc_cause_share * pol_disc_cut + pol_other_share
rows.explainer: Each group of wins: the share of the country it covers × the share of wrongful convictions with the cause it acts on × the cut it makes; plus the other laws and precedents. About 1%.

rows.label: Years of wrongful imprisonment averted a year once the reforms are in force
rows.explainer: Innocent people kept out of prison each year by the window's reforms (equivalently, wrongful prison-years averted a year).

rows.label: Extra compensation paid to exonerees a year under the compensation laws won in fiscal years 2021-2025 (US$)
rows.explainer: Florida's 2025 law opened compensation to 18 exonerees barred before; Oklahoma's replaced a $175,000 cap with $50,000 for every year of wrongful incarceration (annual report 2025, p. 14); other states improved theirs in the window. At up to $50,000 a year served and some 16 years served, a few newly eligible exonerees a year is a few million dollars. Our judgment: $4M a year, from $1M to $12M.

source.title: Innocence Project, Annual Report 2025, compensation in Florida and Oklahoma (p. 14 of the PDF)

rows.label: US exonerations an innocence organisation took part in, 2024

source.title: Criminal Legal News (April 2025), Nearly 150 Exonerations in 2024 Highlight Persistent Flaws in U.S. Criminal Justice System (reporting the National Registry of Exonerations' 2024 annual report)
source.quote: IOs, typically nonprofit legal groups, participated in 53 cases

rows.explainer: The innocence organisations' exonerations in a recent year (of 147 in all), mostly by members of the Innocence Network. The Registry's own report sits behind a bot check, so the figure is from a report of it.

rows.label: People other innocence organisations free from prison a year
rows.explainer: The innocence organisations' exonerations less the Innocence Project's own (counted in the first branch), times the same share still in prison when freed.

rows.label: Years in prison a freed client would otherwise have served
rows.explainer: The clients are 45 on average when exonerated, after 16 years inside (data page); most are serving life or decades-to-life for murder or rape (one of fiscal year 2024's, 50 years to life), and parole boards rarely release people who maintain their innocence. Some would have been paroled or died within a few years. Our judgment: 12 more years, from 5 to 25 (the rest of a 45-year-old's life in prison is about 25 to 30). Whether others would have freed them sooner is a separate question, in the counterfactual below.

source.title: Innocence Project, Explore the Numbers (exonerations data page)

rows.label: Life satisfaction regained per year out of prison (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: The shared figure for what a year in prison costs in life satisfaction (facts/incarceration.json), read by every model that frees people or keeps them out.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person freed (the years they would have served, discounted)
rows.explainer: The life satisfaction regained over the years they would have spent inside (capped by survival), discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Years of life lost per extra year in prison, late in a long term
rows.explainer: The shared figure for people already serving long terms (0.75 years, 0.25 to 1.5): Patterson's 2 years per year comes from short terms and can't run on linearly over a dozen more years at the end of sixteen.

rows.label: Remaining life expectancy of a person in prison
rows.explainer: The shared remaining life of a person freed around 45-50 after a long term (26 years), to match the ages at which these deaths are valued; the reform branch keeps the younger prison population's 40 years.

rows.label: Years a freed person would have spent inside, capped by the life they had left
rows.explainer: The years still to serve, unless prison would have ended their life first: each year inside costs ex_life_years_lost of life, so a person with ex_remaining_life years left dies inside after ex_remaining_life / (1 + years lost a year) years.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person freed (share of a death)
rows.explainer: The years of life the years inside would have cost, as a share of the remaining life: the share of a death each person freed is spared. With the survival cap on the years inside it stays below one death.

rows.label: Remaining life expectancy of a person in prison
rows.explainer: The shared figure for the prison population (mostly in their thirties and forties) that the reforms act on.

rows.label: Years of life lost per year in prison (shorter terms)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (Patterson 2013, New York parolees): each year in prison shortens life by about 2 years, for the shorter terms reforms avert.

rows.label: Reforms: deaths averted per year of imprisonment averted
rows.explainer: Years of life lost per prison-year over the prison population's remaining life, valued at ages 15-49 below.

rows.label: Value of a death averted among exonerees (ages 50-54)
rows.explainer: Exonerees are 45 on average when freed (data page) and the deaths a prison-year causes come years later, so the deaths fall in their fifties: the shared value of a death at 50-54, times the shared multiplier.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the deaths a prison-year causes
rows.explainer: The excess deaths come after the prison-year (shared figure, 3 years), discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person freed, in units of value
rows.formula: ex_deaths_per_freed * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, ex_years_inside) / ex_years_inside * ex_death_delay_discount * ex_value_per_death
rows.explainer: The share of a death spared, spread over the years they would have served and discounted as those years come (and for the wait after each), times the value of a death at their ages.

rows.label: Share of the freed who were under sentence of death
rows.explainer: 9% of the Innocence Project's 257 clients freed or exonerated were sentenced to death (data page); of the window's named exonerees none were on death row, while its death-row clients (Melissa Lucio, Robert Roberson, Richard Glossip) won stays and new hearings but not yet freedom. Our judgment: 4%, from 0 to 10%.

source.title: Innocence Project, Explore the Numbers (exonerations data page)

rows.label: Chance a death-sentenced client would have been executed if not freed
rows.explainer: Most US death sentences end in a reversal, resentencing, commutation or a death from other causes rather than an execution (Gross et al. 2014: most death-sentenced defendants are removed from death row within decades); our reading of the Death Penalty Information Center's counts is that about one in six sentenced since the 1970s has been executed (a judgment, not a quoted figure). Our judgment: 20%, from 5% to 40%. Those who would have been executed would have served about as long before it (the 10 years below) as the others' remaining terms, so their prison-years are counted as for the others.

source.title: Death Penalty Information Center, facts and research (outcomes of death sentences); Gross et al. (2014), PNAS

rows.label: Years until the execution would have come
rows.explainer: Executions come after decades of appeals; a client freed after long years on death row is closer to one. Our judgment: 10 years, from 3 to 20.

source.title: Gross et al. (2014), PNAS (time on death row before execution or removal)

rows.label: Executions averted per person freed, in units of value
rows.explainer: The share on death row times the chance of execution, valued as a death at the same ages and discounted for the wait.

rows.label: Share of exonerees who receive state compensation or a civil settlement
rows.explainer: Most states and the federal government have compensation laws, with bars (guilty pleas, prior records, short filing windows) the Innocence Project campaigns against: Florida's barred 18 exonerees until 2025 (annual report 2025, p. 14); civil suits succeed for some. Our judgment: half are paid, from 25% to 80%. No national count of exonerees paid was found; the share is ours.

source.title: Innocence Project, Annual Report 2025, compensation in Florida and Oklahoma (p. 14 of the PDF)

rows.label: Average compensation paid to an exoneree who is paid (US$)
rows.explainer: Laws like Oklahoma's new one pay $50,000 for every year of wrongful incarceration (annual report 2025, p. 14), the federal standard too; with 16 years served on average that is $800,000, while capped or older state laws pay much less and civil settlements more. Our judgment: $600,000, from $200,000 to $1.5M.

source.title: Innocence Project, Annual Report 2025, compensation in Oklahoma (p. 14 of the PDF)

rows.label: Years until compensation is paid
rows.explainer: Claims take a few years to file and settle: from exoneration for the Innocence Project's own clients, from a law's passage for the compensation laws' newly eligible exonerees. Our judgment: 3 years, from 1 to 6.

source.title: Innocence Project, Annual Report 2025 (Florida's filing window raised from 90 days to two years, p. 14 of the PDF)

rows.label: Years over which an exoneree's household lives on the award
rows.explainer: The award is consumed over the rest of a 45-year-old's life rather than at once. Our judgment: 25 years, from 15 to 35.

rows.label: Consumption per person in an exoneree's household (US$ a year)
rows.explainer: People leaving prison after decades start with nothing: the shared US survey consumption per person times the poorest fifth's spending share, per person with the shared household sizes, as the site's other US models of people in prison do.

rows.label: Value of an award to the exoneree's household (units of value)
rows.explainer: The award spread over the household's years, a log gain in consumption for each member each year, discounted: the site's one log-income scale at the household's own consumption.

rows.label: Cost of the award to the taxpayers who pay it (units of value)
rows.explainer: Compensation is a transfer from state and local taxpayers: the dollars times the shared cost of public funds, over the payers' consumption (the household survey's mean times the shared payer multiple, the claimants' scale), on the same log scale.

rows.label: Net value of an award: the exoneree's gain less the taxpayers' cost (units of value)
rows.explainer: A transfer counts only for what it is worth more to a poor household than to the taxpayers who fund it.

rows.label: Net value of compensation per exoneration, discounted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The share paid times the net value of an award, discounted for the wait.

rows.label: Life satisfaction regained per year of wrongful imprisonment averted (points)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/incarceration.json).

rows.label: Healthy years per person-year (counted through deaths in units of value instead)
rows.explainer: The health cost of prison is counted as the deaths it causes, in units of value (the shared mortality figure), so nothing here.

rows.label: Income gain per person-year (none counted)
rows.explainer: Earnings lost after release are counted as a side effect (ue_earnings, a shared share of the incarceration value), and the compensation laws as transfers below, so nothing here.

rows.label: Chance the wins hold (already won)
rows.explainer: The reforms counted were won or defended in the window; how long they last is the shared years counted.

rows.label: Years a won reform is counted
rows.explainer: The site's shared years a won reform counts (normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Years from a reform to the prison-years it averts
rows.explainer: A reform changes cases from arrest; a person spared a wrongful conviction is spared it at sentencing a year or two later, and the years averted are the years of the sentence after that, which for the serious crimes behind most wrongful convictions run a decade or more (the prison stock is weighted to long terms). Our judgment: 7 years to the middle of them, from 3 to 12.

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on the 16 years Innocence Project clients served on average (exonerations data page)

rows.label: Discount for the wait
rows.explainer: The wait at the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Discounted years the reforms count
rows.explainer: The shared years counted, discounted, after the wait.

rows.label: Value of a death averted at prison ages
rows.explainer: People spared a wrongful conviction are mostly young (27 on average among the Innocence Project's clients, data page): the shared value of a death at 15-49, as in the site's other prison models.

rows.label: Reforms: deaths averted, a year of spending (units of value, before adjustments)
rows.formula: people_affected_per_year * pol_deaths_per_prison_year * pol_value_per_death * discounted_years * ex_death_delay_discount / campaign_years
rows.explainer: Prison-years averted a year times the deaths each causes and their value, over the discounted years counted, divided among the window's five years of spending.

rows.label: Reforms: life satisfaction regained, a year of spending (WELLBYs, before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Prison-years averted a year times the life satisfaction a year inside costs, over the discounted years counted, divided among the five years.

rows.label: Compensation laws: net value of the extra transfers, a year of spending (units of value, before adjustments)
rows.formula: pol_comp_dollars_per_year * comp_net_uov_per_award / comp_award * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, years_of_impact) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - comp_years_until_paid) / campaign_years
rows.explainer: The extra compensation a year times the net value of a dollar of award (the exoneree's gain less the taxpayers' cost), over the discounted years counted after the wait for payment, divided among the five years.

rows.label: Exonerations: trust that the freed were innocent and the shared figures apply
rows.explainer: Most of the Innocence Project's exonerations rest on DNA evidence and are courts' findings; the shared incarceration figures carry their own ranges. Our judgment: 0.95, from 0.85 to 1.

rows.label: Exonerations: share of the years freed that no one else would have ended
rows.explainer: The Innocence Project takes cases others can't fund (DNA testing, experts, years of litigation), but there are now 74 Network groups and over 100 conviction integrity units in prosecutors' offices (which took part in 62 of 2024's 147 exonerations, National Registry via Criminal Legal News). Our judgment: 75% of the years would not have been ended by others, from 50% to 90%.

source.title: Criminal Legal News (April 2025), Nearly 150 Exonerations in 2024

source.title: The Innocence Project, Inc., Form 990 for the year to 30 June 2025, Schedule D Part XII line 2b and Part XIII line 2a (IRS e-file, object 202630939349301418)
source.note: FY2021 $26.9M, FY2022 $27.4M, FY2023 $32.2M, FY2024 $29.7M: about the same every year of the window. The annual reports print their statement of activities excluding pro bono activities.

rows.explainer: Pro bono work by law firms and other donated services, $31.3M, about as much as the Innocence Project's own spending. Its audited statements' split by programme isn't public (the 990 says the statements are available on request), so the shares below are judgments.

rows.label: Share of the donated services that goes to casework
rows.explainer: Law firms work as co-counsel on clients' cases (Foley & Lardner and Kirkland & Ellis on Rosa Jimenez's, annual report 2024); the rest is litigation, amicus work, donated media and facilities. Our judgment: 60% casework, from 40% to 80%.

source.title: Innocence Project, Annual Report 2024, client stories

rows.label: Share of the donated services that goes to strategic litigation and policy
rows.explainer: Firms also write amicus briefs and bring test cases with the strategic litigation team. Our judgment: 20%, from 5% to 35%.

source.title: charityevals' judgment; Form 990 for the year to 30 June 2025, Part III line 4c (strategic litigation, more than 35 amicus briefs)

rows.label: Exonerations: share of the remaining resources from partner groups and law students
rows.explainer: State innocence groups as co-counsel (the Tennessee Innocence Project on Scott Minton's 2025 exoneration) and Cardozo and NYU law students. Our judgment: 20% of what is left, from 10% to 35%.

source.title: Innocence Project, Annual Report 2025 (p. 3 of the PDF)

rows.label: Reforms: share of the resources from coalition partners
rows.explainer: It led several of the window's campaigns (Indiana with the Notre Dame Exoneration Justice Clinic and the state public defenders; Texas with the Innocence Project of Texas) and joined others (New York's discovery coalition, the state groups behind Florida and Oklahoma's compensation laws), annual report 2025. Our judgment: partners put in half the resources, from 30% to 75%.

source.title: Innocence Project, Annual Report 2025, policy wins (pp. 13-15 of the PDF)

rows.label: Exonerations: the Innocence Project's share of the resources behind them
rows.explainer: The Innocence Project's casework spending (legal services and the research and communications behind it) with overhead, against that plus the pro bono work on cases, less the partners' share (Convention 2).
rows.formula: (legal_services_expenses + other_programme_expenses * other_casework_share) * overhead_ratio / ((legal_services_expenses + other_programme_expenses * other_casework_share) * overhead_ratio + pro_bono_services * pro_bono_casework_share) * (1 - ex_partner_share)

rows.label: Exonerations: share delivered as counted
rows.explainer: An exoneration is a court's order: the people counted were freed.

rows.label: Exonerations: discount for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: the count of exonerations is the Innocence Project's own, but no controlled evaluation measures what freeing a person does; the value of a year in prison comes from observational studies of other prisoners.

rows.label: Exonerations: all adjustments
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Reforms: trust that the reforms cut wrongful convictions as assumed
rows.explainer: The evidence that eyewitness procedures, interrogation limits and discovery cut wrongful convictions is mostly from laboratory studies and case reviews, not field trials of the laws. Our judgment: 0.7, from 0.4 to 1.

rows.label: Reforms: counterfactual (in the years counted)
rows.explainer: That a reform would have come some day is the shared years counted (Convention 5).

rows.label: Reforms: the Innocence Project's share of the coalitions behind them
rows.explainer: Its policy and litigation spending (with the communications and research behind them) with overhead, against that plus the pro bono work on them, less the coalition partners' share (Convention 2).
rows.formula: (litigation_policy_expenses + other_programme_expenses * other_reform_share) * overhead_ratio / ((litigation_policy_expenses + other_programme_expenses * other_reform_share) * overhead_ratio + pro_bono_services * pro_bono_litigation_share) * (1 - pol_coalition_share)

rows.label: Reforms: share of the laws applied in practice
rows.explainer: Police departments adopt lineup and interrogation rules unevenly and compliance is rarely audited. Our judgment: 70%, from 40% to 90%.

rows.label: Reforms: discount for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: the wrongful convictions the reforms avert are our judgment; nothing measures them.

rows.label: Reforms: all adjustments
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Network: trust in the exonerations and the shared figures
rows.explainer: The same question as for the Innocence Project's own exonerations.

rows.label: Network: share of the years freed no one else would have ended
rows.explainer: The same question as for the Innocence Project's own exonerations.

rows.label: Network: the Innocence Project's share of other innocence groups' exonerations
rows.explainer: Its network support unit trains and coaches the Network's groups (twelve in-person trainings, six webinars, coaching for more than 50 organisations, regional summits and the annual conference in fiscal year 2025, Form 990 Part III), and its policy wins and research help them; the groups do the casework with their own lawyers and money. Our judgment: 3% of their results, from 1% to 8%.

source.title: The Innocence Project, Inc., Form 990 for the year to 30 June 2025, Part III line 4d (network support)

rows.label: Network: discount for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: the Innocence Project's share of the groups' results is our judgment.

rows.label: Network: all adjustments
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Side effect: families and children with a parent or partner home, as a share of the incarceration value
rows.explainer: Children and partners of people freed or kept out of prison are spared separation and lost income: the shared share (facts/incarceration.json, Wakefield and Wildeman 2013), 15% of the incarceration value, from 0 to 40%.

rows.label: Side effect: earnings kept after release, as a share of the incarceration value
rows.explainer: Fewer years in prison mean higher earnings after release, which the life-satisfaction gap of the year inside doesn't cover: the shared share (facts/incarceration.json, Western 2002), 10%, from 0 to 30%. An exoneree's record is cleared too; the share is kept as it is.

rows.label: Side effect: crimes averted when an exoneration identifies the real perpetrator, as a share of the exoneration value
rows.explainer: The Innocence Project's 257 cases identified 89 real perpetrators, who had committed 101 more violent crimes while the innocent person was in prison (data page); many are already in prison or old when identified. Our judgment: 5% of the branch's value, from 0 to 20%.

source.title: Innocence Project, Explore the Numbers (exonerations data page)

rows.label: Side effect: guilty people not convicted under the new procedures, as a share of the reform value
rows.explainer: Stricter lineup procedures cut some correct identifications along with the mistaken ones (Clark 2012, Perspectives on Psychological Science), and prosecutors say discovery deadlines get some cases dismissed, so some offenders go free; finding the real offender instead of an innocent one, and shorter pretrial detention under discovery rules, cut the other way. Our judgment: -5% of the branch's value, from -20% to +5%.

rows.label: Evidence (outcome-weighted average of the branches)
rows.formula: (released_people * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) * ex_evidence_adj + pol_death_uov_per_year * pol_evidence_adj + net_freed_per_year * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) * net_evidence_adj) / (released_people * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) + pol_death_uov_per_year + net_freed_per_year * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed))
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches (weighted by their deaths averted, most of the result), for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: Counterfactual (outcome-weighted average of the branches)
rows.formula: (released_people * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) * ex_counterfactual_adj + pol_death_uov_per_year * pol_counterfactual_adj + net_freed_per_year * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) * net_counterfactual_adj) / (released_people * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) + pol_death_uov_per_year + net_freed_per_year * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed))
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches (weighted by their deaths averted, most of the result), for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: Share of the resources (outcome-weighted average of the branches)
rows.formula: (released_people * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) * ex_attribution_share + pol_death_uov_per_year * pol_attribution_share + net_freed_per_year * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) * net_attribution_share) / (released_people * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) + pol_death_uov_per_year + net_freed_per_year * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed))
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches (weighted by their deaths averted, most of the result), for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: Share of the resources
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches (the row above), for reading only: each branch applies its own share.

rows.label: Implementation (outcome-weighted average of the branches)
rows.formula: (released_people * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) * ex_implementation_adj + pol_death_uov_per_year * pol_implementation_adj + net_freed_per_year * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) * 1) / (released_people * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) + pol_death_uov_per_year + net_freed_per_year * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed))
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches (weighted by their deaths averted, most of the result), for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: Missing data (outcome-weighted average of the branches)
rows.formula: (released_people * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) * ex_missing_data_adj + pol_death_uov_per_year * pol_missing_data_adj + net_freed_per_year * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) * net_missing_data_adj) / (released_people * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) + pol_death_uov_per_year + net_freed_per_year * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed))
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches (weighted by their deaths averted, most of the result), for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: All adjustments (outcome-weighted average of the branches)
rows.formula: (released_people * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) * ex_total_adj + pol_death_uov_per_year * pol_total_adj + net_freed_per_year * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) * net_total_adj) / (released_people * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) + pol_death_uov_per_year + net_freed_per_year * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed))
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches (weighted by their deaths averted, most of the result), for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: None beyond the side effects above, which are applied in each branch (families, real perpetrators found, offenders missed by new procedures).

rows.label: Exonerations: WELLBYs a year
rows.formula: released_people * released_value * ex_total_adj * (1 + ue_family + ue_earnings + ue_true_perpetrator)
rows.explainer: People freed a year times the life satisfaction regained, adjusted, with the side effects.

rows.label: Exonerations: deaths, executions and compensation a year (units of value)
rows.formula: (released_people * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) * (1 + ue_family + ue_earnings + ue_true_perpetrator) + ex_exonerations / campaign_years * comp_uov_per_exoneration) * ex_total_adj
rows.explainer: Deaths and executions averted for the people freed, with the side effects, plus the net value of compensation for every exoneree (the already released too), adjusted.

rows.label: Network: WELLBYs a year
rows.formula: net_freed_per_year * released_value * net_total_adj * (1 + ue_family + ue_earnings + ue_true_perpetrator)
rows.explainer: Other groups' freed clients valued like the Innocence Project's own, at its share.

rows.label: Network: deaths, executions and compensation a year (units of value)
rows.formula: (net_freed_per_year * (ex_death_uov_per_freed + ex_execution_uov_per_freed) * (1 + ue_family + ue_earnings + ue_true_perpetrator) + net_freed_per_year / ex_share_in_prison * comp_uov_per_exoneration) * net_total_adj
rows.explainer: As for the Innocence Project's own exonerations, at its share of the groups' results.

rows.label: Reforms: WELLBYs a year
rows.explainer: The reforms' life satisfaction, adjusted, with the side effects.

rows.label: Reforms: deaths and compensation a year (units of value)
rows.formula: pol_death_uov_per_year * (1 + ue_family + ue_earnings + ue_pol_crime) * pol_total_adj + pol_comp_uov_per_year * pol_counterfactual_adj * pol_attribution_share * pol_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The reforms' deaths averted with the side effects, adjusted; plus the compensation laws' net transfers, at the Innocence Project's share and the missing-data step only (the evidence and implementation questions are about lineup and interrogation rules, not payments).

rows.explainer: Deaths, executions and net compensation from the three branches, adjusted, in units of value (the reforms' income term is 0).
